body:
What is superconductivity?

When electricity passes through an ordinary metallic conductor, the conductor offers some resistance to the flow of current. This resistance causes part of the electrical energy to be converted into heat.

Some materials behave very differently when cooled sufficiently.

Superconductivity is a state in which certain materials have zero direct-current electrical resistance when appropriate temperature, magnetic-field and current conditions are satisfied.

The transition occurs when the material is cooled below a characteristic critical temperature, commonly represented by Tc.

Superconductivity is not simply very good electrical conductivity. In the superconducting state, the direct-current resistance becomes zero under the required conditions.

Discovery and key properties

In 1911, the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered superconductivity while studying mercury at very low temperatures.

Two central characteristics are associated with the superconducting state:

  • Zero electrical resistance: A direct current can persist without resistive energy loss in the superconducting material while the superconducting conditions are maintained.
  • Meissner effect: A superconductor expels magnetic flux from its interior when entering the superconducting state under suitable magnetic-field conditions.

The magnetic behaviour is an important distinction between a true superconductor and an idealised conductor that merely has zero resistance.

Conditions required for superconductivity

Cooling below Tc is necessary, but it is not the only condition. Superconductivity can also be destroyed if the applied magnetic field or electric current exceeds the material's relevant critical limit.

Magnetic-field behaviour is not identical in all superconductors. Some type-II superconductors permit magnetic flux to enter in a special form under certain field conditions while superconductivity can still persist. Therefore, the Meissner effect should not be described as unlimited magnetic-field exclusion under every circumstance.

Low-temperature and high-temperature superconductors

The expression high-temperature superconductor can be misleading. It refers to a superconductor with a relatively high critical temperature compared with earlier superconducting materials. It does not mean a material intended to operate inside a hot furnace.

Many high-temperature superconductors are copper-oxide compounds, commonly called cuprates. These include ceramic materials, demonstrating that some ceramics can possess unusual electrical properties.

High-temperature superconductors generally still require substantial cooling. The adjective high is relative to the critical temperatures of other superconductors, not a claim that the material can routinely operate at ordinary atmospheric temperatures.

Important applications

  • Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): Superconducting magnets help generate the strong, stable magnetic fields needed by many MRI systems.
  • Particle accelerators: Superconducting magnets help control charged particle beams.
  • Magnetic levitation: Superconducting magnetic effects can contribute to suitable levitation systems.
  • Electrical equipment: Superconducting cables and machines are of interest where high current capacity and reduced resistive losses are useful.

Superconducting equipment is not automatically energy-free or inexpensive. Refrigeration, insulation, protection and other supporting systems consume resources and can make practical deployment costly.

Distinguishing related material terms

TermDefining characteristicTypical context
SuperconductorZero DC resistance under suitable conditionsMRI magnets and research equipment
SuperalloyUseful mechanical performance at elevated temperaturesGas-turbine components
Refractory ceramicAbility to withstand demanding high-temperature environmentsFurnace linings
Shape-memory alloyRecovery of trained shape under suitable conditionsActuators and specialised medical devices

Prelims focus

  • Superconductivity was discovered in mercury by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911.
  • Superconductors have zero DC electrical resistance under the required operating conditions.
  • The Meissner effect concerns magnetic-flux expulsion under suitable conditions.
  • Critical temperature, critical magnetic field and critical current are relevant limits.
  • Some high-temperature superconductors are ceramic cuprates.
  • Trap: A high-temperature superconductor is not the same as a heat-resistant superalloy or refractory material.

[U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Explains...Superconductivity, discovery, properties and applications, consulted 14 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Flux Lattice in Superconductors and Melting, Meissner effect and type-II behaviour, consulted 14 November 2026.]

body:
From electric cells to modern batteries

An electric cell converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy through chemical reactions. The cell has 2 terminals, conventionally marked positive and negative during discharge.

In strict terminology, a battery may contain multiple connected cells, although everyday language often uses the word battery for a single cell as well.

Modern rechargeable batteries are important because they can store electrical energy in chemical form and release it later. They support mobile phones, electric vehicles, emergency power systems and electricity storage for renewable-energy installations.

Main components of a rechargeable cell

ComponentMain functionImportant distinction
AnodeElectrode where oxidation occurs during dischargeNegative electrode during discharge in a typical rechargeable battery
CathodeElectrode where reduction occurs during dischargePositive electrode during discharge in a typical rechargeable battery
ElectrolyteAllows suitable ions to move internallyDoes not provide the external electronic path
SeparatorKeeps electrodes from directly touching while permitting ion transportHelps prevent an internal electronic short circuit

The terms oxidation and reduction refer to electron transfer. Oxidation is the loss of electrons, while reduction is the gain of electrons.

In electrochemistry, the anode is defined by oxidation and the cathode by reduction. Battery manufacturers commonly retain the discharge-based names for the physical electrodes when describing a rechargeable cell, even during charging, when the reactions reverse.

What happens during discharge?

During discharge, the battery supplies electrical energy to an external device.

  1. At the negative electrode, an oxidation reaction releases electrons.
  2. Electrons travel through the external circuit towards the positive electrode, supplying electrical energy to the connected device.
  3. Charged particles called ions move through the electrolyte inside the cell to maintain electrical balance.
  4. At the positive electrode, a reduction reaction receives electrons.

In a typical lithium-ion cell, lithium ions move from the negative electrode towards the positive electrode through the electrolyte during discharge. Electrons travel between these electrodes through the external circuit.

The electrolyte therefore plays a different role from the copper wire connected to the battery. The electrolyte provides internal ionic conduction; the external wire provides electronic conduction.

What happens during charging?

During charging, an external source of electrical energy drives the electrochemical reactions in the opposite direction. In a typical lithium-ion cell, lithium ions move back towards the negative electrode, where energy is stored chemically for later use.

The stored energy is not a reservoir of free electrons waiting inside the battery. It is associated with the chemical states of the electrode materials and the reversible electrochemical reactions.

Primary and secondary batteries

  • Primary batteries: Intended mainly for discharge rather than repeated recharging. Common examples include ordinary non-rechargeable dry cells.
  • Secondary batteries: Designed so that charging can reverse the main cell reactions sufficiently for repeated use. Lithium-ion and lead-acid batteries are familiar examples.

Rechargeable does not mean unlimited lifetime. Repeated operation, temperature, charging conditions and chemical ageing gradually affect battery performance.

Energy capacity, power and battery life

Energy capacity indicates how much electrical energy a battery can deliver under specified conditions. It is commonly expressed in watt-hours (Wh) or kilowatt-hours (kWh).

Power is the rate at which energy is delivered or absorbed. It is expressed in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW). A battery may store a large quantity of energy but still have limits on how quickly it can supply that energy.

Under ideal conditions, 1 kWh of stored energy corresponds to supplying 1 kW for 1 hour. Actual operating time depends on losses, discharge limits and operating conditions.

Energy density compares stored energy with battery mass or volume. Cycle life describes how many charge-discharge cycles a battery can perform before its performance reaches a specified limiting condition.

Prelims focus

  • During discharge, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
  • For a typical discharging rechargeable cell, the anode is negative and the cathode is positive.
  • Electrolytes conduct ions inside the cell; electrons travel through the external circuit.
  • Separators help prevent direct electrical contact between the electrodes.
  • Primary batteries are mainly non-rechargeable; secondary batteries are rechargeable.
  • Wh and kWh measure energy, whereas W and kW measure power.
  • Trap: The electrolyte does not perform the same function as the external electrical wire.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, electric cells and terminals; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 14, Electric Current and Its Effects, cells and batteries; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, electrical conduction through liquids; U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Explains...Batteries, electrochemical storage and charge movement, consulted 14 November 2026.]

body:
Why lithium-ion batteries are widely used

Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable batteries in which lithium ions move between electrode materials during charging and discharging. They can store substantial energy relative to their size and weight, making them useful where compact or lightweight storage is important.

Lithium-ion batteries are used in smartphones, laptops, electric vehicles and stationary energy-storage systems. However, lithium-ion is a family of battery chemistries rather than one fixed combination of materials.

Where is lithium present in a lithium-ion cell?

In a widely used lithium-ion cell, the negative electrode contains a carbon material such as graphite. The positive electrode contains a lithium-bearing compound.

During charging, lithium ions move towards the negative electrode and are stored within the electrode material. During discharge, they move back towards the positive electrode.

Most conventional lithium-ion cells do not use a sheet of metallic lithium as their negative electrode. Lithium-ion and lithium-metal batteries are related but distinct battery categories.

Important lithium-ion cathode materials

Two widely discussed cathode families are lithium iron phosphate and lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide.

Cathode familyMain cathode constituentsUseful distinction
LFPLithium, iron and phosphateDoes not require nickel or cobalt in the LFP cathode
NMCLithium, nickel, manganese and cobaltUses nickel and cobalt; composition can vary

LFP stands for lithium iron phosphate. It is valued for relatively good thermal stability, long cycle-life potential and avoidance of nickel and cobalt in the cathode. Its energy density is generally lower than that of many high-energy NMC cell designs.

NMC refers to lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide cathode materials. Different NMC formulations have different proportions of nickel, manganese and cobalt, affecting cost, energy density, durability and safety.

Neither family is automatically superior in every application. Battery performance also depends on the negative electrode, electrolyte, separator, cell construction and operating conditions.

Not every lithium-ion battery contains cobalt. An LFP cathode does not contain cobalt or nickel, while an NMC cathode contains both. Both families still rely on lithium.

Applications in renewable-energy storage

Solar and wind generation vary with sunlight and wind conditions. A battery can store some of the electricity produced during periods of available generation and release it when required.

In stationary electricity storage, a suitable battery system can help with short-term balancing, backup supply and shifting electricity use between different times.

Battery storage does not generate primary energy. Its role is to store previously supplied energy and release part of it later, with losses occurring during charging, storage and discharge.

Battery management and thermal safety

Rechargeable batteries must operate within suitable voltage, temperature and current limits. Battery-management systems monitor and control important operating conditions to help reduce overcharging, excessive discharge and unsafe temperatures.

Thermal runaway is a dangerous process in which heat generated inside a battery can accelerate further heat-producing reactions. It may result in rapid temperature rise, release of gases or fire.

Severe physical damage, internal short circuits, excessive temperatures and improper electrical conditions can contribute to dangerous battery failures.

LFP cells generally have better thermal stability than several other lithium-ion cathode chemistries, but this does not make every LFP battery completely fireproof. Safe operation depends on the whole battery system.

Understanding battery performance claims

  • Energy density: Useful when comparing how much energy batteries store relative to mass or volume.
  • Cycle life: Useful when repeated charging and discharging are important.
  • Power capability: Describes the rate at which a system can supply or absorb energy.
  • Safety: Depends on chemistry, cell quality, protection systems and operating conditions.
  • Cost and material availability: Depend partly on the chosen electrode materials and supply chain.

The ideal battery for a lightweight mobile device may therefore differ from the ideal battery for a large stationary installation.

Prelims focus

  • Lithium-ion batteries rely on reversible movement of lithium ions between electrodes.
  • Graphite is a common negative-electrode material.
  • LFP means lithium iron phosphate; its cathode does not require nickel or cobalt.
  • NMC means lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide.
  • Solar and wind battery storage shifts energy between times; it does not create energy.
  • Thermal runaway is a dangerous accelerating heating process.
  • Trap: Lithium-ion batteries do not all have identical cathodes, energy densities or safety characteristics.

[U.S. Department of Energy, DOE Explains...Batteries, charging and discharging, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Reducing Reliance on Cobalt for Lithium-ion Batteries, NMC cathode composition, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Department of Energy, Fast Charging LFP Aerogel Cathode Materials to Eliminate Nickel/Cobalt Reliance, LFP material distinction, consulted 14 November 2026; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Lithium-Ion Battery Recycling Frequently Asked Questions, thermal-runaway and fire risks, consulted 14 November 2026.]
